physical_indicators: Immense size (a true giant); shaped the landscape (credited with creating Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard, Nantucket); left giant footprint-like impressions; a Massachusetts beach (Moshup Beach) is named for him.
paranormal_indicators: None substantiated beyond his origin as a giant; framed as a benevolent culture-hero, not a hidden or feared entity.
full_narrative: Maushop (also spelled Moshup) is one of the most prominent figures in Wampanoag legend, a benevolent giant credited with creating Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard (Noepe), and Nantucket. One version holds he created Martha's Vineyard to escape mainland violence; when homesick, he tried building a bridge back by scattering boulders into the water. Unlike many wildman figures, he is remembered as a folk hero, honored rather than avoided.

physical_indicators: Small stature, ~2-3 feet tall; grey skin, sometimes glowing; oversized features; can transform into a porcupine in some tellings.
paranormal_indicators: Leads travelers astray, clouds memory, lures with mysterious lights; some stories say they persuade people to leap from cliffs; attack with knives or poisoned arrows; fire manipulation and shapeshifting.
full_narrative: Pukwudgies are small trickster woodland spirits in Wampanoag tradition, legends centered on Hockomock Swamp ('place where spirits dwell'), the largest freshwater swamp in Massachusetts. Origin tied to jealousy of the giant Maushop. Morally mixed: capable of helping or teaching, genuinely dangerous when disrespected. Modern 'strange creature' reports tied to the same swamp reflect the 20th-century Bridgewater Triangle paranormal tradition (coined by Loren Coleman, 1970s) layered on top of the older material. A separate Wampanoag term, Nikommo, also appears in source lists for 'little people' -- not yet independently researched.

entity_nature: Giant wildman -- the linguistic origin of the word 'Sasquatch' itself
physical_indicators: 6-9 feet tall, covered in dark hair/fur; footprints described around 20 inches long; generally seen singly.
paranormal_indicators: Some traditions describe touch causing unconsciousness, abduction, a rudimentary shared language with captives, and the ability to grant 'guardian spirit' power/strength to certain people -- documented by ethnographer Wilson Duff among others.
full_narrative: Sasq'ets, from the Halq'emeylem language of Coast Salish peoples (Sts'ailes, Sto:lo, and related Fraser Valley/lower BC nations), is the actual linguistic root of the modern word 'Sasquatch' -- popularized by J.W. Burns in a 1929 Maclean's article after collecting community accounts. Generally described as a powerful but generally benign supernatural being. Regional variants exist across Coast Salish groups (e.g. Squee'noos and Papay'oos among Nanaimo-area Coast Salish). A recovered prior research script adds: Coast Salish tradition describes Sasq'ets traveling between dense timber belts without leaving obvious paths, using whistles, rock-throwing, and heavy wood-knocks to communicate across steep valleys -- consistent with, and a good independent echo of, the app's own tracked behavior categories.

paranormal_indicators: Attempts to abduct people in some legends; man-eater in others; deliberately avoided by the Choctaw in areas where one has been seen.
full_narrative: The Shampe is a malevolent, ogre-like monster of Choctaw folklore, sometimes a giant, sometimes described as hairy like an ape. Its most distinctive trait is its overpowering smell, said to make it nearly impossible to fight. Lives deep in the forest in a cave no Choctaw has found. Attracted by the smell of blood, and known to follow wounded game or hunters. A closely related figure, Lofa, appears in neighboring Chickasaw tradition (name means 'flayer/skinner'). Native-languages.org explicitly cautions against lumping all Native 'giant hairy being' traditions together as interchangeable Bigfoot names -- worth respecting that distinction rather than flattening it.

entity_name: Tsul 'Kalu (also known as Judaculla; also: Kee-lah-nah)
region_label: Appalachian Mountains (North Carolina / Tennessee / Western Carolina highlands)
physical_indicators: Giant with long, tangled hair; glowing/reddish eyes; enormous strength; keen eyesight; leaves large footprint-like impressions in soil and rock. Judaculla Rock, a National Register of Historic Places soapstone petroglyph site near Cullowhee, NC (verified coordinates above), is directly tied to his legend. Recorded by Europeans as early as 1823.
paranormal_indicators: Said to read thoughts and control minds at will; described as able to leap across entire mountains in a single motion; dwells in a specific named place, Tsunegun'yi.
full_narrative: Tsul 'Kalu ('he has them slanting/sloping', referring to his eyes), also called Judaculla or the Cherokee Devil, is a giant, hairy figure of Cherokee mythology, the great lord of the hunt, invoked in hunting rites and rituals. Generally respected rather than feared, a guardian of respectful hunting -- though some versions describe him turning hostile after being insulted. Multiple independent modern sources explicitly connect him to Bigfoot folklore directly. In plural form, also names a traditional race of giants said to dwell farther west.

region_label: Northeast Woodlands / New York & Great Lakes region
entity_nature: Malevolent giant (cannibalistic; defeated in a great war, not currently 'at large')
physical_indicators: Described as gigantic men with skin covered in stone or hardened mud so tough that arrows would bounce off; tall, fierce, immensely strong.
paranormal_indicators: Some tellings describe wounds self-healing/regenerating; origin accounts describe them as ordinary humans transformed by supernatural means, not a natural species.
full_narrative: The Stonish Giants (Ot-ne-yar-heh, or Ge-no-sqwa in Seneca) are documented as early as 1828 by Tuscarora historian David Cusick, and again in 1881 by Tuscarora Chief Elias Johnson. Described as a powerful, hostile tribe from the wilderness who invaded Haudenosaunee lands, cannibalistic, devouring entire towns, until the Confederacy fought a great war and drove them back into the wilderness/northwest. Unlike Sasq'ets or Tsul'Kalu, this is framed as a historical war narrative against a defeated enemy, not an ongoing wildman tradition -- an important structural difference worth keeping distinct. A recovered prior research script adds: described as throwing boulders and breaking heavy branches as territorial warnings.

region_label: Southwest / Mount Taylor (Tsoodzil) area, New Mexico
entity_nature: Primordial mythic-age monster (structurally different from an ongoing wildman tradition -- see honest caveat below)
physical_indicators: Immense size -- his stride said to cover the distance a man could walk from sunrise to noon; associated with specific rock formations near Mount Taylor said to be his remains.
paranormal_indicators: Origin from either the sun god or unnatural conception with a stone father; one of the Anaye ('Alien Monsters') of the mythic age; ultimately slain by the Hero Twins using lightning and sunbeam arrows.
full_narrative: Ye'iitsoh ('Big Monster' or 'Big God') is the most feared of the Anaye in Navajo tradition, from the Diné Bahane' creation narrative. Threatened to wipe out early humanity through predation before being defeated by the Hero Twins (Monster Slayer and Born for Water). HONEST CAVEAT: several pop-culture sources loosely call this 'the Navajo Sasquatch,' but the actual story structure is meaningfully different from Sasq'ets/Tsul'Kalu/Stonish Giants -- Ye'iitsoh is a primordial being already defeated in the deep mythic past and tied to specific geology, not an ongoing forest-dwelling wildman that might still be encountered today. Filed here for completeness, but this structural difference should not be flattened away.

region_label: Southwestern United States / Zuni Pueblo, New Mexico
entity_nature: Giant cannibalistic demon — myth-time antagonist, ultimately defeated by the twin war gods (structurally similar caveat to Ye'iitsoh: not an ongoing wildman tradition)
physical_indicators: Several times larger than a normal human; torso as big as a large elk's; long grey hair as stiff as porcupine quills; skin so thick the knuckles appear horned; muscular arms covered in black-and-white scales; bulging red eyes that never blink; some tellings add long yellow tusks and talons.
paranormal_indicators: A demon/spiritual being by nature; an inveterate liar; uses trickery and false kinship claims to lure victims.
full_narrative: Documented since 1901 by ethnographer Frank Hamilton Cushing in 'Zuni Folk Tales,' based on his direct fieldwork living among the Zuni from 1879-1884 -- primary-source ethnographic quality, comparable to Mooney's Cherokee work. Átahsaia lures two young maidens by pretending to be their grandfather, tries to feed them soup made of human children, and is ultimately killed by the twin Zuni war gods, who skin him and make an effigy from his hide. HONEST CAVEAT: like Ye'iitsoh, this is a myth-time antagonist already defeated in the origin stories, not a currently-encountered wildman like Sasq'ets or Tsul'Kalu -- worth keeping that structural difference visible.
